title: First-Order Stationarity of Reverse Diffusions

paper.title: First-Order Stationarity of Reverse Diffusions
paper.abstract: Abstract Recent literature has shown a strong connection between optimization and sampling. We develop the corresponding first-order theory for diffusion models. First, the SDE-based reverse-time flows of overdamped and underdamped Langevin diffusions contract relative Fisher divergences at explicit exponential rates whenever the stationary potential of the forward process is strongly convex—a condition on the noising process one chooses, not on the data. This is a unique advantage of SDE-based reverse diffusion, absent in the reverse process based on ODEs. Second, we incorporate discretization and establish averaged first-order stationarity bounds—the sampling analog of averaged gradient-norm guarantees in nonconvex optimization—for samplers of both overdamped and underdamped diffusion models. As in nonconvex optimization, the convexity-free certificate is local: it guarantees score consistency, not global mode weights.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text:
Diffusion models generate data in two stages: a forward Markov process gradually corrupts samples from an unknown data distribution ρ 0 ho_{0} until their law is essentially a tractable stationary distribution, and generation simulates this process backward in time, guided by the score functions ∇ log ⁡ ρ s

Three approximations separate the implemented sampler from the ideal reverse process—initialization from the reference law rather than the true terminal marginal, time discretization, and score estimation—and a large body of work bounds their combined effect on the terminal law, in total variation, KL, or Wasserstein distance. This paper takes a different, more structural view. Rather than asking how far the final sample is from the data, we ask what the reverse dynamics itself—exact or discretized—does to a first-order measure of mismatch. sections.heading: Why first-order guarantees?
sections.text: In smooth nonconvex optimization one cannot certify convergence to a global minimum, yet gradient descent still admits the averaged guarantee 1 N ​ ∑ k ‖ ∇ f ​ ( x k ) ‖ 2 ≲ f ⁡ ( x 0 ) − f ⋆ η ​ N + O ⁡ ( η ) \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k}\|\nabla f(x_{k})\|^{2}\lesssim\frac{f(x_{0})-f^{\star}}{\eta N}+O(\eta) ( Ghadimi and Lan, 2013 ) . The sampling situation is parallel: for non-log-concave data, converting score accuracy into KL or total-variation convergence requires functional inequalities, whereas the relative Fisher divergence remains meaningful without such assumptions —driving it to zero certifies that the sampler’s law is locally consistent with its target, the two scores agreeing on average in L 2 L^{2} . The analogy also makes the limitation transparent: as a stationary point need not be a minimum, a law can have small relative Fisher divergence while misallocating mass between well-separated modes. This limitation parallels the gap between stationarity and global optimality in nonconvex optimization.

sections.heading: Convergence theory of diffusion models.
sections.text: Time reversal of diffusions goes back to Anderson (1982) and Haussmann and Pardoux (1986) ; diffusion models build directly on this theory, including the critically damped kinetic variant of Dockhorn et al. (2022) . A growing line of quantitative convergence theory controls initialization, discretization, and score-estimation errors simultaneously for essentially arbitrary data distributions ( Lee et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023b ; Jiao et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: Connections between sampling and optimization.
sections.text: A complementary line of work draws connections between sampling dynamics and optimization. The classical variational formulation of the Fokker–Planck equation interprets overdamped Langevin dynamics as a Wasserstein gradient flow of the relative entropy ( Jordan et al., 1998 ) , motivating the viewpoint of sampling as optimization over the space of probability measures ( Wibisono, 2018 ) . Momentum-based sampling admits an even closer analogy with accelerated optimization: Ma et al. (2021) interpreted underdamped Langevin dynamics as an analog of Nesterov acceleration for minimizing the KL divergence, with hypocoercivity playing a role analogous to the coupling between position and momentum in accelerated optimization.

sections.heading: Fisher-divergence contraction.
sections.text: Recent work has also studied the evolution of Fisher divergence along isotropic Fokker–Planck channels. Wibisono (2026) established contraction of Fisher divergence under suitable convexity assumptions. Closest in spirit to our work, Balasubramanian et al. (2022) developed Fisher-information guarantees for forward Langevin Monte Carlo, viewing Fisher divergence as a sampling analog of first-order stationarity in optimization. Our work develops a corresponding perspective for reverse-time diffusion, where contraction must be established against a reference that itself evolves.

sections.heading: Contraction in continuous reverse flow.
sections.text: Our results form two groups, one about exact reverse flows and one about discrete samplers. If the stationary potential U U of the forward diffusion is strongly convex, then the reverse SDE contracts score mismatch exponentially, for both overdamped and underdamped diffusion. The assumptions concern only the forward potential, and no log-Sobolev inequality is imposed on the data: the continuous reverse dynamics forgets initialization error exponentially fast for almost arbitrary data.

sections.heading: Averaged Fisher divergence bound for discretized algorithms.
sections.text: (i) For the frozen-score exponential integrator of the reverse overdamped process—the idealized DDPM-type update—with spatially Lipschitz scores and sub-Gaussian data assumptions, the numerical law p ^ t \hat{p}_{t} satisfies 1 T ∫ 0 T ℱ ( p ^ t ∥ q t ) d t ≲ H 0 / T + L s 2 d h + O ( h 2 ) \frac{1}{T}\int_{0}^{T}\mathcal{F}(\hat{p}_{t}\,\|\,q_{t})\,\mathrm{d}t\lesssim H_{0}/T+L_{s}^{2}dh+O(h^{2}) against the exact reverse marginals q t q_{t} (Theorem 4.5 ). (ii) For the critically damped reverse process we prove an averaged bound on the full phase-space relative Fisher divergence (Theorem 5.5 ), with the sampler compared to the twin chain that pushes the exact initialization through the same numerical kernels, so that the bound isolates the initialization error.

sections.heading: Organization.
sections.text: Section 2 fixes the setting; in Section 3 , we give results for continuous reverse flows. In Sections 4 and 5 , we give results for discrete samplers of the overdamped and underdamped model separately. Section 6 gives our experiment results. Appendices A – D prove the results of Sections 2 – 5 in order, and Appendix E collects critical-damping identities. Our work focuses on the process mechanism itself, so we analyze initialization error and discretization error. Throughout the paper we assume we have access to the true score functions.

sections.heading: Underdamped: a modified Fisher divergence contracts.
sections.text:
The underdamped flow dissipates only the velocity components of the relative score (Corollary 2.2 ), so position-direction error can be damped only indirectly , by rotating into the velocity directions through the Hamiltonian coupling. Following the hypocoercivity paradigm ( Villani, 2009 ) , we therefore measure the error in a quadratic form with position–velocity cross terms , chosen so that the coupling converts the conserved part of the error into the dissipated part. sections.heading: 5 Averaged stationarity of the discretized critically damped reverse
sections.text: We now prove the underdamped counterpart of Theorem 4.5 , for the critically damped kinetic OU forward process: the underdamped model ( 2.4 ) with U ⁡ ( x ) = 1 2 ​ ‖ x ‖ 2 U(x)=\tfrac{1}{2}\|x\|^{2} and the parameters γ = 2 \gamma=2 , ξ = 1 \xi=1 , and for the frozen-score exponential integrator. One genuine obstacle separates this case from Section 4 . Repeating the argument of Section 4 along the frozen-score SDE interpolation is possible, but it could only provide a bound on ℱ v ( p ^ t ∥ q t ) \mathcal{F}_{v}(\hat{p}_{t}\,\|\,q_{t}) , as in Proposition 2.5 . To upgrade ℱ v \mathcal{F}_{v} to the full ℱ \mathcal{F} one wants a hypocoercive Lyapunov functional in the spirit of Ma et al. (2021) ; but differentiating ℱ P ( p ^ t ∥ q t ) \mathcal{F}_{P}(\hat{p}_{t}\,\|\,q_{t}) along an SDE interpolation like ( 4.2 ) produces derivatives of the score mismatch, objects for which no useful control is available. Our resolution is decomposing the integrator. Since the frozen-score step solves a linear SDE, it can be written as a deterministic score kick applied at the beginning of the step, followed by the score-free reverse dynamics d ​ Y = C ​ Y ​ d ​ τ + 2 ​ E ​ d ​ W \,\mathrm{d}Y=CY\,\mathrm{d}\tau+2E\,\mathrm{d}W run for the full step (Lemma D.1 ). Along this interpolation no derivative of the score error ever appears: the kick is a deterministic map, and the score-free leg is an exact linear diffusion on which entropy and twisted-Fisher identities hold in closed form. Therefore, hypocoercive dissipation and discretization decouple completely. However, this decoupled composition also forces us to tell the story in an indirect way. Instead of bounding ℱ ( p ^ t ∥ q t ) \mathcal{F}(\hat{p}_{t}\,\|\,q_{t}) directly, we will bound ℱ ( p ^ t ∥ q ^ t ) \mathcal{F}(\hat{p}_{t}\,\|\,\hat{q}_{t}) for a reference process q ^ t \hat{q}_{t} , which isolates the initialization error. The discretization is isolated in the difference between q ^ t \hat{q}_{t} and q t q_{t} , and it is controlled at the level of path measures by the standard Girsanov computation ( Chen et al., 2023b ) .

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: Reverse diffusions admit a first-order theory that parallels smooth optimization line by line. The relative score is the gradient; the SDE reverse flow is its descent dynamics, dissipating KL and contracting Fisher divergences exponentially under strong log-concavity of the forward stationary potential—a condition on the noising process one chooses, not on the data. Under mild assumptions, implementable integrators then achieve averaged first-order stationarity at rate H 0 / T H_{0}/T plus explicit step-size terms. This also separates the two standard samplers. Only the SDE descends, and the ODE is a change of variables, so it forgets nothing of its initialization. Since the identities of Section 2 hold from any time on, the same holds for any perturbation of the law introduced during sampling: the SDE forgets it in the first-order sense, the ODE carries it to the end. This gives a precise form to the observation that stochastic samplers correct earlier errors ( Karras et al., 2022 ) and to the role of Langevin corrector steps in ODE-based samplers ( Song et al., 2021 ; Chen et al., 2023a ) . However, the stationarity guarantee for the underdamped reverse process is indirect. Theorem 5.5 compares the sampler p ^ \hat{p} with a twin chain q ^ \hat{q} that pushes the exact initialization through the same numerical kernels, so it isolates the initialization error. This is the price of decoupling the analysis of discretization and hypocoercivity, and Assumption 5.2 is also an artifact of this compromise. Even though we have KL ( Q 0 : T ∥ Q ^ 0 : T ) ≤ O ~ ( h ) \operatorname{KL}\left(Q_{0:T}\,\|\,\hat{Q}_{0:T}\right)\leq\tilde{O}(h) , it does not automatically transfer to a control on ℱ ( p ^ t ∥ q t ) \mathcal{F}(\hat{p}_{t}\,\|\,q_{t}) . Closing this gap—a first-order comparison of the kinetic sampler with the exact reverse process itself—is a natural direction for future work. As the dictionary predicts, a first-order certificate is local: a law can have small relative Fisher divergence while misallocating mass between well-separated modes, so our guarantees certify local consistency with the target rather than recovery of mode weights—the price of convexity-free guarantees, in sampling as in nonconvex optimization. A log-Sobolev inequality for the data plays the role of the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition ( Polyak, 1963 ; Karimi et al., 2016 ) : when it holds, the Fisher divergence bounds then convert into KL bounds against the reference laws: the first-order theory recovers zeroth-order convergence exactly when a PL-type inequality holds, as in optimization.

sections.text: Throughout this appendix, p ^ i \hat{p}_{i} and q ^ i \hat{q}_{i} are the grid laws of the numerical chain started from p ^ 0 \hat{p}_{0} and from the exact initialization q ^ 0 = ρ T \hat{q}_{0}=\rho_{T} respectively, p ^ i , τ \hat{p}_{i,\tau} and q ^ i , τ \hat{q}_{i,\tau} are their within-step interpolations ( 5.8 ), and C C , E E , Π v \Pi_{v} , D D are the matrices of ( 5.1 ). Assumption 5.3 supplies the positive densities and the finite H 0 H_{0} , F 0 F_{0} of the standing conventions; since q ^ 0 = q 0 \hat{q}_{0}=q_{0} , H 0 = KL ( p ^ 0 ∥ q ^ 0 ) H_{0}=\operatorname{KL}(\hat{p}_{0}\,\|\,\hat{q}_{0}) and F 0 = ℱ ( p ^ 0 ∥ q ^ 0 ) F_{0}=\mathcal{F}(\hat{p}_{0}\,\|\,\hat{q}_{0}) . The argument follows the two-factor form ( 5.7 ) of the integrator. The kick is a deterministic map applied to both laws, so it preserves relative entropy and transforms the relative score by the inverse transpose of its Jacobian (Lemma D.2 ). The score-free leg is a linear diffusion, along which relative entropy dissipates the velocity part of the relative score, and a twisted Fisher divergence with a time-dependent metric can dissipate the full relative score, at the price of a term involving the mixed Hessian of the reference law, which Assumption 5.2 controls (Proposition D.3 ). Appendix D.4 combines the two into a Lyapunov functional, lists the four properties (M1)–(M4) that the moving metric must have, and shows that they make the functional decrease at least as fast as ℱ ( p ^ i , τ ∥ q ^ i , τ ) \mathcal{F}(\hat{p}_{i,\tau}\,\|\,\hat{q}_{i,\tau}) along each leg and match at the grid points, so that the bound telescopes (Proposition D.4 ). Appendix D.5 motivates and defines the metric, verifies (M1)–(M3), and completes the proof of the theorem; the remaining property (M4), a 2 × 2 2\times 2 matrix inequality, is verified in Appendix D.6 .

sections.heading: Motivation.
sections.text: By ( D.5 ), relative entropy dissipates only the velocity part ℱ v \mathcal{F}_{v} of the relative score. To reach the full ℱ \mathcal{F} we add, as in the hypocoercive functional of Section 3 , a twisted Fisher divergence ℱ M \mathcal{F}_{M} . Identity ( D.6 ) shows what each ingredient contributes along a leg: the drift term ⟨ g , ( M ˙ − C ​ M − M ​ C ⊤ ) ​ g ⟩ \left\langle g,(\dot{M}-CM-MC^{\top})g\right\rangle is the only one that can dissipate in every direction, including position; the trace term has the right sign as soon as M ⪰ 0 M\succeq 0 ; and the mixed-Hessian term has no sign, but by Assumption 5.2 it costs only a multiple of ℱ v \mathcal{F}_{v} , which the entropy pays. A constant metric does not survive the kick. By ( D.3 ), the kick replaces the metric M M by ( ∇ Ψ ) − 1 ​ M ​ ( ∇ Ψ ) − ⁣ ⊤ (\nabla\Psi)^{-1}M(\nabla\Psi)^{-\top} , which can be larger than M M in some directions. We therefore let the metric move within each leg: it starts at a matrix M ⁡ ( 0 ) M(0) slightly below a fixed grid metric Θ \Theta , low enough that the increase by the kick is absorbed by the decrease in the metric Θ − M ⁡ ( 0 ) \Theta-M(0) , and returns to Θ \Theta at the end of the leg, so that consecutive legs match at the grid points. The deficit Θ − M ⁡ ( 0 ) \Theta-M(0) is a budget that the dissipation along the leg must pay back.

sections.heading: Setting.
sections.text: Let x 1 , … , x n ∈ [ − 1 , 1 ] d x_{1},\dots,x_{n}\in[-1,1]^{d} be the n = 28000 n=28000 training images of CelebA-HQ ( Karras et al., 2018 ) at 256 × 256 256\times 256 resolution, and ρ 0 = 1 n ​ ∑ i δ x i \rho_{0}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}\delta_{x_{i}} . The OU marginals are ρ s = 1 n ​ ∑ i N ⁡ ( a s ​ x i , b s 2 ​ I d ) \rho_{s}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i}N(a_{s}x_{i},b_{s}^{2}I_{d}) with a s = e − s a_{s}=e^{-s} , b s 2 = 1 − e − 2 ​ s b_{s}^{2}=1-e^{-2s} —a Gaussian kernel density estimate whose bandwidth is the noise level—and ∇ log ⁡ ρ s ​ ( y ) = a s ​ x ¯ s ​ ( y ) − y b s 2 , x ¯ s ​ ( y ) = ∑ i w i s ​ ( y ) ​ x i , w s ​ ( y ) = softmax i ⁡ ( 2 ​ a s ​ ⟨ y , x i ⟩ − a s 2 ​ ‖ x i ‖ 2 2 ​ b s 2 ) \nabla\log\rho_{s}(y)=\frac{a_{s}\bar{x}_{s}(y)-y}{b_{s}^{2}},\ \ \bar{x}_{s}(y)=\sum_{i}w_{i}^{s}(y)\,x_{i},\ \ w^{s}(y)=\operatorname{softmax}_{i}\Big(\frac{2a_{s}\langle y,x_{i}\rangle-a_{s}^{2}\|x_{i}\|^{2}}{2b_{s}^{2}}\Big)\! (the common term ‖ y ‖ 2 \|y\|^{2} is dropped from the softmax), where x ¯ s ​ ( y ) = 𝔼 ⁡ [ X 0 ∣ X s = y ] \bar{x}_{s}(y)=\mathbb{E}[X_{0}\mid X_{s}=y] is the posterior mean. One score evaluation is one matrix product with the n × d n\times d data matrix. Since the data are exactly memorized, every trajectory ends at a training image, and what the initialization can change is which training images are produced. That the samples are training images is not a shortcoming of the experiment but the setting of the paper, which assumes the true score throughout: for a finite training set the true score is the empirical one above, and it is also the exact minimizer of the denoising score-matching objective, so a diffusion model whose network fitted its objective perfectly would memorize; the generalization of trained models comes from the inductive bias of the network, not from the objective ( Yoon et al., 2023 ; Gu et al., 2025 ; Kadkhodaie et al., 2024 ; Li et al., 2024 ) . Using the exact score is therefore the only way to run the object analyzed in Sections 3 – 4 on real data with the score error removed, leaving initialization and discretization as the only error sources. The phenomenon shown here is moreover not tied to memorization: Appendix F.4 shows the same phenomenon with a learned score that does not memorize.

sections.text: We use the frozen-score exponential integrator ( 4.3 ) on a grid of forward times s 0 = T > s 1 > ⋯ > s K − 1 = s min > s K = 0 s_{0}=T>s_{1}>\dots>s_{K-1}=s_{\min}>s_{K}=0 that is geometric in the noise-to-signal ratio σ s = e 2 ​ s − 1 \sigma_{s}=\sqrt{e^{2s}-1} ( Karras et al., 2022 ) between s 0 = T s_{0}=T and s K − 1 = s min s_{K-1}=s_{\min} , followed by one last step to s = 0 s=0 ( K = 150 K=150 , s min = 1 × 10 − 5 s_{\min}=1\times 10^{-5} , T = 5.06 T=5.06 ). The horizon is T = 5.06 T=5.06 , the horizon of the DDPM noise schedule used in Appendix F.4 , so that the two experiments run the same three initial laws over the same time span; at this T T the standard initialization is close to exact ( KL ( N ( 0 , I d ) ∥ ρ T ) = 0.30 \operatorname{KL}(N(0,I_{d})\,\|\,\rho_{T})=0.30 nats) and serves as the control. Each initialization is run for 64 64 samples.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Figure 3 shows the 64 64 generated images of each run. Every one of them is close to a training image (root-mean-square distance to the nearest training image below one gray level, i.e. the noise of the last step): local consistency holds regardless of the initialization. Which training images are produced does depend on the initialization. The standard initialization N ⁡ ( 0 , I d ) N(0,I_{d}) , nearly exact at this horizon ( H 0 = 0.30 H_{0}=0.30 nats), is the control: it returns a mixed draw of the training set—dark and light backgrounds, hair colors and lighting conditions (mean pixel value − 0.14 -0.14 on the [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] scale, mean per-image pixel standard deviation 0.51 0.51 ). The mean shifts ( H 0 = 5.03 H_{0}=5.03 resp. 6.78 6.78 nats) move the output to opposite ends of the training set: β = − 4 \beta=-4 returns almost exclusively dark photographs—dim lighting, dark backgrounds, hair and skin (mean pixel value − 0.43 -0.43 )—and β = + 4 \beta=+4 almost exclusively bright ones—light backgrounds, blond hair, pale skin, over-exposed shots. The initialization error is not negligible but shrinks along the flow in the first-order sense, yet it decides the palette of the output: small relative Fisher divergence certifies local consistency, not the mode weights. sections.heading: F.4 The same effect with a learned score
sections.text: To check that this phenomenon persists in the presence of score estimation errors, we repeat the mean-shift experiment with the pretrained CelebA-HQ 256 × 256 256\times 256 DDPM of Ho et al. (2020) ( google/ddpm-celebahq-256 ), sampled with its ancestral sampler ( 250 250 steps)—the discrete predecessor of the integrator of Section 4 —whose noise schedule corresponds to the OU horizon T = 5.06 T=5.06 . Figure 4 shows 64 64 samples from the standard initialization N ⁡ ( 0 , I d ) N(0,I_{d}) and from N ⁡ ( μ , I d ) N(\mu,I_{d}) with μ = β ​ 1 / d \mu=\beta\,\mathbf{1}/\sqrt{d} for β = − 4 \beta=-4 and + 4 +4 —the same three initial laws as in Figure 3 . The mean pixel value of the samples moves from − 0.09 -0.09 to − 0.56 -0.56 and + 0.50 +0.50 respectively: a positive shift makes the learned model return bright photographs and a negative shift dark ones. The bias now acts on the cluster of bright (dark) photographs rather than on individual training images, as one expects from a score that has learned the data distribution rather than the training set; the mechanism—the mass allocated to the clusters is decided by the tilt the initialization induces, while every sample remains a clean face—is the same. Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Contents Reading mode Colour theme License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2609.31612v1 [stat.ML] 25 Sep 2026 First-Order Stationarity of Reverse Diffusions Zhifeng Chen † † thanks: Email: zchen925@wisc.edu Chenyang Jiang Yazhen Wang Affiliation: Department of Statistics, UW-Madison Abstract Recent literature has shown a strong connection between optimization and sampling. We develop the corresponding first-order theory for diffusion models. First, the SDE-based reverse-time flows of overdamped and underdamped Langevin diffusions contract relative Fisher divergences at explicit exponential rates whenever the stationary potential of the forward process is strongly convex—a condition on the noising process one chooses, not on the data. This is a unique advantage of SDE-based reverse diffusion, absent in the reverse process based on ODEs. Second, we incorporate discretization and establish averaged first-order stationarity bounds—the sampling analog of averaged gradient-norm guarantees in nonconvex optimization—for samplers of both overdamped and underdamped diffusion models. As in nonconvex optimization, the convexity-free certificate is local: it guarantees score consistency, not global mode weights. 1 Introduction Diffusion models generate data in two stages: a forward Markov process gradually corrupts samples from an unknown data distribution ρ 0 ho_{0} until their law is essentially a tractable stationary distribution, and generation simulates this process backward in time, guided by the score functions ∇ log ⁡ ρ s 
abla\logho_{s} of the forward marginals, learned by (denoising) score matching ( Hyvärinen, 2005 ; Vincent, 2011 ; Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Song and Ermon, 2019 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2021 ) . Three approximations separate the implemented sampler from the ideal reverse process—initialization from the reference law rather than the true terminal marginal, time discretization, and score estimation—and a large body of work bounds their combined effect on the terminal law, in total variation, KL, or Wasserstein distance. This paper takes a different, more structural view. Rather than asking how far the final sample is from the data, we ask what the reverse dynamics itself—exact or discretized—does to a first-order measure of mismatch. The central objects are the relative score and the relative Fisher divergence : for positive densities p p and q q , ℱ ( p ∥ q ) = 𝔼 p ∥ ∇ log p q ∥ 2 . \mathcal{F}(p\,\|\,q)=\mathbb{E}_{p}\Big\|
abla\log rac{p}{q}\Big\|^{2}. The relative score vanishes identically if and only if p = q p=q , so ℱ ( p ∥ q ) \mathcal{F}(p\,\|\,q) is a natural stationarity measure: it plays the role of the squared gradient norm ‖ ∇ f ‖ 2 \|
abla f\|^{2} , as KL ( ⋅ ∥ q ) \operatorname{KL}(\cdot\,\|\,q) plays that of the objective value f f . The analogy is not merely formal. The Fokker–Planck equation of overdamped Langevin dynamics is the gradient flow of relative entropy in the Wasserstein geometry ( Jordan et al., 1998 ) , and the relative Fisher divergence is exactly its gradient norm. We will show in this work that this is also true for the reverse flow: d d ​ t KL ( p t ∥ q t ) = − ℱ ( p t ∥ q t )  rac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}t}\operatorname{KL}(p_{t}\,\|\,q_{t})=-\mathcal{F}(p_{t}\,\|\,q_{t}) (Corollary 2.2 )—the exact analog of the descent identity d d ​ t ​ f ​ ( x t ) = − ‖ ∇ f ​ ( x t ) ‖ 2  rac{\,\mathrm{d}}{\,\mathrm{d}t}f(x_{t})=-\|

Most rows of this dictionary are not new: they underlie the first-order theory of forward Langevin Monte Carlo ( Balasubramanian et al., 2022 ) and Fisher-information dissipation along forward flows ( Wibisono, 2026 ) . The contribution of this paper is that the dictionary survives time reversal, where the reference law q t q_{t} is no longer a fixed stationary distribution but a moving target set by the noising schedule. We show that this symmetry holds for both overdamped and underdamped reverse-time SDEs, but does not extend to their probability flow ODE counterparts. Why first-order guarantees? In smooth nonconvex optimization one cannot certify convergence to a global minimum, yet gradient descent still admits the averaged guarantee 1 N ​ ∑ k ‖ ∇ f ​ ( x k ) ‖ 2 ≲ f ⁡ ( x 0 ) − f ⋆ η ​ N + O ⁡ ( η )  rac{1}{N}\sum_{k}\|
abla f(x_{k})\|^{2}\lesssim rac{f(x_{0})-f^{\star}}{\eta N}+O(\eta) ( Ghadimi and Lan, 2013 ) . The sampling situation is parallel: for non-log-concave data, converting score accuracy into KL or total-variation convergence requires functional inequalities, whereas the relative Fisher divergence remains meaningful without such assumptions —driving it to zero certifies that the sampler’s law is locally consistent with its target, the two scores agreeing on average in L 2 L^{2} . The analogy also makes the limitation transparent: as a stationary point need not be a minimum, a law can have small relative Fisher divergence while misallocating mass between well-separated modes. This limitation parallels the gap between stationarity and global optimality in nonconvex optimization. 1.1 Related work Convergence theory of diffusion models. Time reversal of diffusions goes back to Anderson (1982) and Haussmann and Pardoux (1986) ; diffusion models build directly on this theory, including the critically damped kinetic variant of Dockhorn et al. (2022) . A growing line of quantitative convergence theory controls initialization, discretization, and score-estimation errors simultaneously for essentially arbitrary data distributions ( Lee et al., 2023 ; Chen et al., 2023b ; Jiao et al., 2025 ) . Connections between sampling and optimization. A complementary line of work draws connections between sampling dynamics and optimization. The classical variational formulation of the Fokker–Planck equation interprets overdamped Langevin dynamics as a Wasserstein gradient flow of the relative entropy ( Jordan et al., 1998 ) , motivating the viewpoint of sampling as optimization over the space of probability measures ( Wibisono, 2018 ) . Momentum-based sampling admits an even closer analogy with accelerated optimization: Ma et al. (2021) interpreted underdamped Langevin dynamics as an analog of Nesterov acceleration for minimizing the KL divergence, with hypocoercivity playing a role analogous to the coupling between position and momentum in accelerated optimization. Fisher-divergence contraction. Recent work has also studied the evolution of Fisher divergence along isotropic Fokker–Planck channels. Wibisono (2026) established contraction of Fisher divergence under suitable convexity assumptions. Closest in spirit to our work, Balasubramanian et al. (2022) developed Fisher-information guarantees for forward Langevin Monte Carlo, viewing Fisher divergence as a sampling analog of first-order stationarity in optimization. Our work develops a corresponding perspective for reverse-time diffusion, where contraction must be established against a reference that itself evolves. 1.2 Contributions and paper organization Contraction in continuous reverse flow. Our results form two groups, one about exact reverse flows and one about discrete samplers. If the stationary potential U U of the forward diffusion is strongly convex, then the reverse SDE contracts score mismatch exponentially, for both overdamped and underdamped diffusion. The assumptions concern only the forward potential, and no log-Sobolev inequality is imposed on the data: the continuous reverse dynamics forgets initialization error exponentially fast for almost arbitrary data. Averaged Fisher divergence bound for discretized algorithms.
